## Audit Entry

The append-only record of what happened to a contract: `action` (an enum — created,
submitted, approved, approved with conditions, rejected, delegated, on hold,
resumed, signed, amended, renewed, terminated), `doneBy` linked to an **Employee**,
`occurredAt`, the `subject` it concerns, plus `note` and `conditions`.

```ts
import { AuditEntry, auditActionLabel, auditActionHue } from '../audit-entry';
@field trail = linksToMany(AuditEntry);
```

**Why it is its own card, not a `containsMany` on Contract.** An audit trail's whole value
is that it cannot be rewritten by the thing it describes. Held on the contract, "who
approved this and when" would be as mutable as the contract body — exactly the claim an
auditor is testing. A separate card gives each event a stable address that survives edits
to its subject.

**`subjectTitle` is a deliberate snapshot.** Reading the title through `subject` shows
today's name; an audit entry must say what the thing was called when the decision was made.
So the link is for navigation and the stored title is the record.

**`doneBy`, not `actor`.** The edit form takes its label from the field name, and "Actor" is
a system word that makes readers ask what it means. "Done by" reads correctly for every
action in the vocabulary.

### Non-goals

Does not enforce append-only — the realm has no immutable-record primitive, so this is a
convention the consuming app keeps, not a guarantee the storage makes. Says so in the card.
Does not own approval routing (**ApprovalChainField** does) or the decision UI (the
consuming app does). Does not authenticate the actor: identity is supplied by the consumer,
because a card cannot read the signed-in user.
